title: Percentage questions in an aptitude test
summary: Recognise the common ways percentage questions are asked and answer them quickly without falling into the usual traps.
learningObjectives: Spot the pattern in a percentage question
keyTakeaways: A rise of x% then a fall of x% does not return to the start
Convert percentages to fractions to calculate faster
explanation:
Most percentage questions reduce to a few patterns. Spend your first seconds working out **which pattern it is**, then use a shortcut for it.

This is a SAMPLE lesson for testing the layout, so the sections are generic. For a real exam, check its official syllabus and notices.

blocks.title: How percentage questions are usually asked

patterns.name: Successive change
patterns.asked: A price rises by 20% and then falls by 20%. What is the net change?
patterns.trap: Assuming the two cancel out to zero.

patterns.name: Percent of the wrong base
patterns.asked: A is 25% more than B. By what percent is B less than A?
patterns.trap: Answering 25% instead of switching the base.
patterns.tip: Write B = 100, A = 125, then compare 25 with 125.

patterns.name: Reverse percentage
patterns.asked: After a 20% discount the price is 400. What was the original price?
patterns.tip: The sale price is 80% of the original: 400 ÷ 0.8 = 500.

blocks.note: General patterns, not real past questions. Check the official syllabus and notices.

commonMistakes: Using the wrong base when the question reverses the comparison
Adding percentages that apply to different bases
Not checking whether the question asks for a change or a final value

quiz.question: A price rises 10% then falls 10%. Compared with the start it is:
After a 25% discount an item costs 300. The original price was:
quiz.explanation: The sale price is 75% of the original: 300 ÷ 0.75 = 400.

quiz.question: A is 50% more than B. B is what percent less than A?
quiz.explanation: If B = 100, A = 150; the gap of 50 is 33.3% of 150.

socraticChallenge.scenario: You have 90 seconds for a percentage question and have spent 60 without a method.
socraticChallenge.question: Do you keep going or skip?
socraticChallenge.idealAnswer: Skip and return if there is time; note the pattern that stalled you, then practise that pattern separately.

exercises.prompt: A shirt is marked up 40% on cost and sold at a 10% discount. What is the profit percent on cost?
exercises.answer: 1.4 × 0.9 = 1.26, so the profit is 26% on cost.

exercises.prompt: A salary rises 20% to 7,200. What was it before?

reviewCards.prompt: What is the first question to ask in any percentage problem?
reviewCards.answer: Percent of what, that is, which number is the base.

reviewCards.prompt: How do you combine two successive percentage changes?
